name: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (post-traumatic)
populations: adults after head trauma or concussion
summary: Brief spinning vertigo triggered by head position, caused by displaced otoconia in a semicircular canal, usually the posterior one. Common after head trauma. Diagnose with Dix-Hallpike, treat with the Epley manoeuvre.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: A single Epley manoeuvre resolved vertigo in 56% versus 21% with sham or control (OR 4.42, 5 trials); about 36% recur after treatment

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Dix-Hallpike: vertigo with torsional, upbeating nystagmus confirms posterior canal BPPV. Supine roll test for the horizontal canal

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Not needed when BPPV criteria are met and there are no atypical features; imaging is for central or head-injury red flags

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: Lifetime prevalence 2.4% in adults; 8% of 1378 BPPV patients at one tertiary centre had a traumatic cause

keyFacts.label: After head injury
keyFacts.value: Of 179 people with dizziness after mild traumatic brain injury, 10.6% had positional vertigo and BPPV was confirmed in 9

overview:
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is an inner ear disorder characterised by repeated episodes of positional vertigo [r1]. In the usual model, otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) detach from the utricular macula and settle in a semicircular canal. When the head moves into the provoking position, the crystals move under gravity and drag the canal fluid, which deflects the sensory cupula and gives a false signal of rotation. The result is a short burst of spinning vertigo with a characteristic nystagmus. It is common after head trauma, but most BPPV is idiopathic [r2,r3].

The posterior canal is the most common site. In a post-traumatic series, 68.2% had posterior canal BPPV and about 27% had horizontal canal BPPV [r4]. The diagnosis is clinical, made with the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre for the posterior canal and the supine roll test for the horizontal canal [r1,r5]. The Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre is safe and effective for posterior canal BPPV [r6,r1]. Post-traumatic BPPV may need more manoeuvres than idiopathic BPPV, and the evidence on recurrence is conflicting [r7,r2,r4].

Physiotherapists should rule out central causes and cervical vascular pathology before testing, especially when vertigo is continuous rather than positional (HINTS), or follows neck trauma [r8,r9,r10].

epidemiology.text: In a nationally representative German survey, BPPV accounted for 8% of adults with moderate or severe dizziness or vertigo. Lifetime prevalence was 2.4%, 1-year prevalence 1.6% and 1-year incidence 0.6%. The median duration of an episode was 2 weeks, 86% of affected people sought care, interrupted daily activities or took sick leave, and only 8% received effective treatment [r11]. After head trauma, positional vertigo is common: in 179 patients with vertigo, dizziness or imbalance after mild traumatic brain injury, 19 (10.6%) had attacks elicited by position change, BPPV was confirmed in 9 and judged highly probable in 10 [r12]. At one tertiary centre, 110 of 1378 patients with BPPV (8%) had a traumatic cause (symptom onset within 30 days of head trauma) [r2]. A review notes that post-traumatic BPPV has a more prolonged and refractory course than idiopathic BPPV, and can coexist with vestibular migraine, post-concussive dizziness or central vestibular dysfunction [r3].

intrinsic: Older age, migraine, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and stroke were each independently associated with BPPV in the population survey (associations, not proven causes) [r11]
In a tertiary series, traumatic BPPV patients were younger than idiopathic cases (mean 61 versus 65 years) and more often male (40% versus 27%) [r2]
A coexisting vestibular migraine, post-concussive dizziness or central vestibular condition can complicate diagnosis and recovery [r3]
extrinsic: Head trauma, from mild concussion to severe traumatic brain injury, is a recognised cause; the proposed mechanisms are direct mechanical disruption of the otolithic organs, altered endolymph dynamics or vascular compromise [r3]
Trauma-related BPPV was more often bilateral (32% versus 19% in idiopathic BPPV) [r2]
Delayed diagnosis and treatment: only 8% of affected participants in the survey had received effective treatment [r11]

mechanism.summary: In post-traumatic BPPV, a blow to the head or a sudden deceleration shakes the otolith organs. Otoconia detach from the utricular macula, travel through the common crus and settle in the most dependent canal, the posterior canal, where they collect in the long arm. When the head is tipped back and turned (as in lying down, rolling over or looking up), the crystals move under gravity and drag the canal endolymph, which deflects the cupula and triggers vertigo and nystagmus. This is the accepted canalithiasis model. The mechanical disruption of the otolithic organs after trauma is proposed rather than proven in people [r3].
sequence: A head impact, fall or sudden deceleration jars the skull and the inner ear [r3].
Otoconia detach from the utricular macula, and some drift into the posterior canal through the common crus.
The crystals settle in the long arm of the posterior canal, the lowest part of the canal in the upright head.
The person lies back, rolls in bed, looks up or bends, and the head moves into the provoking position.
The crystals fall through the canal under gravity, dragging the endolymph and deflecting the cupula in the ampulla.
The brain receives a false rotation signal, producing brief spinning vertigo and torsional, upbeating nystagmus with nausea [r1].
The crystals settle, the vertigo stops within about a minute, and it returns with the next provoking movement.

variants.name: Posterior canal BPPV
variants.description: The most common type. Dix-Hallpike provokes vertigo with torsional, upbeating nystagmus. Treated with canalith repositioning (Epley) [r1,r6]. In one post-traumatic series, 68.2% were posterior canal [r4].

variants.name: Horizontal (lateral) canal BPPV
variants.description: Positional vertigo with horizontal nystagmus, found on the supine roll test when Dix-Hallpike shows horizontal or no nystagmus [r1]. Made up about 27% of one post-traumatic series (geotropic 22.7%, apogeotropic 4.5%) [r4].

variants.name: Bilateral or multicanal BPPV
variants.description: More common after head trauma, with both ears affected in 32% of traumatic cases versus 19% of idiopathic cases [r2].

variants.name: BPPV coexisting with concussion
variants.description: Dizziness after concussion has many causes. BPPV can sit alongside vestibular migraine, cervical and oculomotor problems, and can be missed unless positional tests are done [r3,r12].

anatomy.text: The bony labyrinth of the inner ear contains the three semicircular canals (anterior, posterior and lateral), the utricle and saccule, and the cochlea. Each canal ends in an ampulla containing the cupula, which senses fluid movement during head rotation. The utricle and saccule carry the maculae, where otoconia sit on a gel layer and sense linear acceleration and gravity. The posterior canal opens into the utricle through the common crus, which is the route by which displaced otoconia enter it. The vestibular nerve carries the signals to the brainstem.

structures.name: Utricle and utricular macula
structures.role: Sense linear acceleration and head tilt. The normal home of the otoconia

structures.name: Otoconia
structures.role: Calcium carbonate crystals on the macula. When displaced into a canal they cause BPPV

structures.name: Posterior semicircular canal
structures.role: Senses head rotation in the plane of the canal. The most commonly affected canal, because it is the most dependent in the upright and supine head [r4]

structures.name: Lateral (horizontal) semicircular canal
structures.role: Senses head turns in the horizontal plane. Affected in about one quarter of post-traumatic BPPV in one series [r4]

structures.name: Anterior semicircular canal
structures.role: Rarely affected; vertical canal in the plane of the Dix-Hallpike movement

structures.name: Cupula and ampulla
structures.role: Sensory end organ of each canal. Deflected by the moving endolymph that the falling crystals drag

structures.name: Vestibular nerve
structures.role: Carries signals from the canals and otolith organs to the brainstem and cerebellum

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
BPPV is a mechanical disorder of the labyrinth rather than an injury to its nerve. Displaced otoconia in a semicircular canal move when the head moves into the provoking position, drag the endolymph and deflect the cupula, which produces vertigo and nystagmus that start after a short delay, last less than a minute and fade with repetition. After head trauma, the otolithic organs are thought to be disrupted mechanically, endolymph dynamics are altered, or the blood supply to the inner ear is compromised, which can release otoconia [r3].

Post-traumatic BPPV may be harder to treat. A meta-analysis of six retrospective cohorts (865 traumatic and 3027 idiopathic patients) found that traumatic BPPV needed more repositioning manoeuvres (RR 3.27, 95% CI 1.88–5.69) and recurred more often (RR 2.91, 95% CI 2.04–4.14) [r7]. A tertiary centre series of 1378 patients found no association between trauma and resolution or recurrence (overall resolution 76%, recurrence 38%), and a trauma-centre series found more manoeuvres were needed (mean 2.0 versus 1.3) but similar recurrence [r2,r4]. The evidence is therefore mixed on recurrence.

structures.name: Utricular macula
structures.effect: Otoconia detach after trauma or with age, and drift into the canal system [r3]

structures.name: Posterior semicircular canal
structures.effect: Receives the crystals through the common crus; they settle in the long arm and move when the head tips back [r1]

structures.name: Cupula
structures.effect: Deflected by the fluid drag, giving a false rotation signal

structures.name: Vestibular nerve and brainstem
structures.effect: Normally intact. They transmit the false signal, producing vertigo and nystagmus; central pathways are not the primary lesion

muscles.name: Extraocular muscles
muscles.effect: Driven by the vestibulo-ocular reflex to produce the torsional, upbeating nystagmus of posterior canal BPPV [r1]

muscles.name: Neck muscles
muscles.effect: Protective guarding from fear of provoking movement, which can restrict range and aggravate neck pain or headache

muscles.name: Postural and trunk muscles
muscles.effect: Impaired balance and fall risk in older or frail patients, which the guideline asks clinicians to assess [r1]

cellular.description: Crystals break from the macular gel layer after a head impact or deceleration [r3].
Detached crystals travel through the common crus into the posterior canal and settle in the long arm.

cellular.timing: Median episode about 2 weeks if untreated
cellular.description: Each provoking movement moves the crystals and produces brief vertigo. The median duration of an episode was 2 weeks in a population survey [r11].
After repositioning, the Dix-Hallpike test converted from positive to negative in many more treated patients than controls (OR 9.62, 95% CI 6.0–15.42) [r6].

systems.effect: The primary system. Positional vertigo and nystagmus from a canal mechanical problem [r1].
Normally intact. Central causes of vertigo, including stroke, must be excluded with the HINTS examination when vertigo is continuous [r8].
Nausea occurred in 16.7%–32% of patients during repositioning manoeuvres [r6].
Some patients could not tolerate the manoeuvres because of cervical spine problems [r6].
86% of affected people sought care, interrupted daily activities or took sick leave; fear of movement and fall risk follow [r11,r1].

grading.system: Classification by canal and mechanism (Bárány Society diagnostic criteria) [r5]

grades.description: Vertigo with torsional, upbeating nystagmus provoked by the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre; the commonest form [r1,r4].
grades.prognosis: Responds to canalith repositioning (Epley); recurrence is common

grades.description: Positional vertigo with horizontal nystagmus on the supine roll test; geotropic (towards the ground) or apogeotropic (away from the ground) [r1,r4].
grades.prognosis: Treated with horizontal-canal manoeuvres; may be less predictable

grades.description: Rare. Typically vertical (downbeating) nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike testing; not covered in the guideline abstract reviewed.
grades.prognosis: Treated with manoeuvres directed to the anterior canal; evidence was not reviewed for this page

grades.description: Both ears or more than one canal affected, more common after trauma [r2].

timeframes.summary: Each episode of vertigo lasts well under a minute, but the underlying problem can last weeks if untreated (median episode 2 weeks). A manoeuvre often resolves it within one to a few sessions, and the guideline advises reassessment within 1 month [r11,r1].

healing.description: Detachment at trauma and migration into the posterior canal over hours to days [r3]
Median episode duration was 2 weeks in a population survey; many resolve spontaneously, some persist [r11]
A positive Dix-Hallpike converts to negative in most treated patients; the Epley was no better than Gans after 1 week [r6,r13]
Reassess within 1 month to document resolution or persistence, and evaluate persistent symptoms [r1]
About 36% recurred after treatment in the Cochrane review, and 38% in a tertiary series [r6,r2]

milestones.label: Dix-Hallpike negative after Epley
milestones.note: Conversion to a negative test favoured Epley over sham or control (OR 9.62) [r6]

milestones.label: Epley comparable to Gans at 1 week
milestones.note: Epley was superior to Gans at 24 hours but not after 1 week; low to very low certainty [r13]

milestones.label: Median untreated episode
milestones.note: Median duration of an episode was 2 weeks [r11]

milestones.label: Guideline reassessment
milestones.note: Reassess within 1 month of observation or treatment [r1]

timeframes.returnToSport: Return to sport follows resolution of positional vertigo and recovery of balance, and in concussion it follows the concussion return-to-sport pathway. Avoid collisions, heading or work at height until positional vertigo has cleared and the person can move without dizziness (clinical convention).

symptoms: Brief episodes of spinning vertigo (usually under a minute) triggered by lying down, rolling over in bed, looking up, bending forwards or turning the head quickly [r11]
Nausea, sometimes vomiting, and a sense of unsteadiness for hours afterwards
A short delay between the movement and the vertigo, and fading with repeated movement
A history of head trauma, fall or concussion in the preceding days to weeks in post-traumatic BPPV [r2]
No hearing loss, tinnitus or new neurological symptoms with the positional attacks (their presence suggests another cause)
Fear of moving the head and a reduction in daily activity, driving or work [r11]
signs: Torsional, upbeating nystagmus provoked by the Dix-Hallpike test toward the affected ear in posterior canal BPPV [r1]
Horizontal nystagmus on the supine roll test in horizontal canal BPPV [r1]
Reproduction of the patient's vertigo during the provoking position, with nausea [r6]
Normal neurological examination, cranial nerves and cerebellar tests, with no central signs
Impaired balance in some patients, especially older adults [r1]

subjective: Timing and mechanism of any head injury, and the interval between injury and the onset of positional vertigo (traumatic BPPV was defined as onset within 30 days) [r2]
Provoking movements and duration: lying down, rolling over, looking up, bending; episodes under a minute point to BPPV rather than continuous vertigo [r11]
Associated features: hearing loss, tinnitus, headache, visual change, double vision, speech or limb symptoms, which suggest another diagnosis [r1]
Continuous vertigo lasting hours to days (acute vestibular syndrome), which needs a central screen and not BPPV testing alone [r8]
Migraine history and previous BPPV; coexisting concussion symptoms such as headache and cognitive difficulty [r3]
Factors that modify management: impaired mobility or balance, central nervous system disorder, lack of home support and fall risk [r1]
Neck history: injury, pain, arterial risk factors and any limitation of neck extension, because the test positions load the neck [r9,r6]
observation: Spontaneous nystagmus and gaze-evoked nystagmus in upright posture (indicating a central or acute peripheral problem)
Gait and balance on entering the room, tandem stance and turning
Eye movement quality: smooth pursuit, saccades and skew
Behaviour: avoidance of head movement, or a rigid neck position
palpation: Cervical spine tenderness and upper cervical joint tenderness, particularly after trauma
Facial or temporal bone tenderness after significant head trauma
rangeOfMotion: Active neck extension and rotation: check range and tolerance before the Dix-Hallpike or any position that puts the neck into extension and rotation [r6,r9]
If the neck cannot tolerate the position, use a modified test (side-lying) or refer [r14,r6]
strength: Not a primary feature; screen limb power for central causes
Lower limb strength and balance in older or frail patients with fall risk [r1]
neuro: Cranial nerves, facial symmetry, hearing screen, and eye movements
Cerebellar tests: finger-nose, heel-shin, rapid alternating movements and tandem gait
Head impulse, nystagmus and test of skew (HINTS) when vertigo is continuous rather than positional [r8]
Neurological signs, severe headache or neck pain after trauma: stop and escalate rather than test [r8,r10]
functional: Balance tests: tandem stance, single-leg stance, and gait with head turns
Fall risk and ability to manage at home; consider home safety [r1]
Provocation in daily movements: lying down, rolling in bed, looking up, bending

specialTests.name: Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre
specialTests.procedure: Bring the patient from upright sitting to supine with the head turned 45° to one side and the neck extended about 20°, with the affected ear down. Watch the eyes (ideally with video goggles) for nystagmus and ask about vertigo for at least 30 seconds. Return to sitting and watch for reversal, then repeat on the other side.
specialTests.positive: Vertigo with torsional, upbeating nystagmus, with a short delay, lasting less than a minute and fading on repetition. Estimated sensitivity 79% (95% CI 65–94) and specificity 75% (33–100) in a single study with very weak methodology, so the test is the reference standard for posterior canal BPPV and its own accuracy is poorly established.

specialTests.name: Side-lying test
specialTests.purpose: Alternative positional test for patients who cannot move into the Dix-Hallpike position
specialTests.procedure: The seated patient is rapidly tipped onto one side with the head turned 45° up, then returned to sitting and tested on the other side.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of vertigo with positional nystagmus. In the single study identified, sensitivity was 90% (95% CI 79–100) and specificity 75% (33–100), with very weak methodology and limited validity.

specialTests.name: Supine roll test
specialTests.procedure: With the patient supine and the head flexed about 30°, turn the head 90° to each side and observe for horizontal nystagmus, noting whether it beats toward the lower ear (geotropic) or away (apogeotropic).
specialTests.positive: Positional vertigo with horizontal nystagmus. The guideline recommends this test when the history is compatible with BPPV and Dix-Hallpike shows horizontal or no nystagmus. Accuracy figures were not identified in the sources reviewed.

specialTests.name: HINTS examination (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew)
specialTests.purpose: Screen for stroke in continuous (acute vestibular syndrome) vertigo; not a test for BPPV
specialTests.procedure: Perform the horizontal head impulse test, observe nystagmus in primary and eccentric gaze, and perform the alternate-cover test for skew deviation. It applies to continuous vertigo with nystagmus, in a patient at stroke risk, and requires training.
specialTests.positive: A normal horizontal head impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus in eccentric gaze, or skew deviation indicates a central cause. In 101 high-risk patients with acute vestibular syndrome, this was 100% sensitive and 96% specific for stroke, and early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging missed 12% (all within 48 hours).

specialTests.name: Cervical vascular and tolerance screen before neck positioning
specialTests.purpose: Identify patients at risk of vascular pathology of the neck before manoeuvres that extend and rotate the neck
specialTests.procedure: Take a history for neck pain, headache, trauma and vascular risk, and adapt the examination to explore a vasculogenic hypothesis. Assess neck range and tolerance of extension and rotation before positional tests.
specialTests.positive: Recent neck trauma, new neck pain or headache with dizziness, or other signs suggesting vascular pathology: do not perform neck-extending positional tests; arrange urgent medical assessment. Accuracy figures were not identified.

clinicalRules.name: AAO-HNSF BPPV guideline: diagnosis
clinicalRules.description: Diagnose posterior canal BPPV when vertigo with torsional, upbeating nystagmus is provoked by Dix-Hallpike (head turned 45°, neck extended 20°, affected ear down). Perform a supine roll test if the history fits and Dix-Hallpike shows horizontal or no nystagmus [r1].

clinicalRules.name: AAO-HNSF BPPV guideline: management
clinicalRules.description: Strong recommendations: treat posterior canal BPPV with a canalith repositioning procedure, and no post-procedure postural restrictions. Recommended against routine imaging, vestibular testing and vestibular suppressant drugs [r1].

clinicalRules.name: Bárány Society diagnostic criteria
clinicalRules.description: Operational criteria for BPPV that include established and emerging syndromes by canal and mechanism [r5].

outcomeMeasures.name: Dix-Hallpike conversion (positive to negative)
outcomeMeasures.use: Objective outcome of repositioning. Conversion favoured Epley over sham or control (OR 9.62, 95% CI 6.0–15.42) [r6].

outcomeMeasures.name: Patient-reported vertigo (visual analogue scale or symptom diary)
outcomeMeasures.use: Complete resolution of vertigo was the primary outcome in the Cochrane review; track episodes and triggers [r6]

outcomeMeasures.name: Dizziness Handicap Inventory
outcomeMeasures.use: Impact on daily life, used in dizziness research after concussion and with neck problems (clinical convention)

outcomeMeasures.name: Falls and balance measures
outcomeMeasures.use: The guideline asks clinicians to assess fall risk and mobility in all patients with BPPV [r1]

imaging.indication: The guideline recommends against radiographic imaging and vestibular testing for patients who meet BPPV criteria without atypical features [r1]
Acute head-injury red flags, central signs on HINTS, severe headache or new neurological deficit, or atypical or non-resolving positional vertigo
imaging.findings: Excludes haemorrhage, fracture and posterior circulation stroke; early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging can be falsely negative [r8]

imaging.indication: Hearing loss, otorrhoea, haemotympanum or suspected temporal bone fracture after head trauma

differentials.name: Concussion with dizziness
differentials.distinguishing: Dizziness, headache and cognitive symptoms without clear positional provocation or the typical nystagmus; BPPV can coexist [r3].

differentials.name: Persisting post-concussion symptoms
differentials.distinguishing: Dizziness with multiple other drivers (neck, oculomotor, exertional, mood); BPPV is one treatable cause that should be tested for [r12].

differentials.name: Cervicogenic dizziness
differentials.distinguishing: Unsteadiness linked to neck pain or neck movement rather than head position relative to gravity; a diagnosis of exclusion [r10].

differentials.name: Cervical arterial dysfunction or vertebral artery dissection
differentials.distinguishing: Neck pain or headache with vertigo, visual or brainstem symptoms after trauma or neck movement; urgent medical care [r10,r9].

differentials.name: Vestibular migraine
differentials.distinguishing: Recurrent vertigo with migraine features and photophobia; the commonest cause of neck pain with vestibular symptoms [r10].

differentials.name: Vestibular neuritis and other acute vestibular syndromes
differentials.distinguishing: Continuous vertigo for days with spontaneous nystagmus; HINTS separates peripheral from central causes [r8].

differentials.name: Posterior circulation stroke or central positional vertigo
differentials.distinguishing: Atypical nystagmus (vertical or direction-changing), central HINTS signs, ataxia or other neurological signs; imaging [r8].

differentials.name: Labyrinthine concussion or perilymph fistula
differentials.distinguishing: Hearing loss, tinnitus and continuous vestibular symptoms after head trauma; needs ENT assessment.

redFlags: Continuous vertigo (not brief and positional) with new neurological signs, severe headache, double vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, limb weakness or numbness, or inability to walk: emergency. Suspect stroke or other central cause and arrange same-day assessment; use HINTS in acute vestibular syndrome [r8].
Direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, a normal head impulse test with spontaneous nystagmus, or skew deviation: treat as central until proven otherwise and refer urgently [r8].

Neck pain or headache with vertigo, especially after trauma or neck movement: suspect vertebral artery dissection. Do not perform neck-extending positional tests or manual therapy, and arrange urgent medical assessment [r10,r9].

Head-injury red flags after trauma (worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, drowsiness, focal signs, neck pain, signs of skull fracture or CSF leak): manage on the concussion emergency pathway before any vestibular testing.
Sudden hearing loss, haemotympanum or fluid from the ear after head trauma: possible temporal bone fracture or labyrinthine injury; refer for urgent ENT assessment.
Positional vertigo that does not respond to repeated manoeuvres, or persists beyond 1 month: re-evaluate for unresolved BPPV, other peripheral vestibular disorders or central causes [r1].
Patients who cannot tolerate neck positions because of cervical spine problems, or who have significant fall risk: modify or refer rather than force the manoeuvre [r6,r1].

Serious adverse events, mostly vascular, have been reported after conservative neck procedures; stop and escalate for any sharp new neck pain, headache, nausea or neurological change during or within 48 hours after testing [r15].

management.principles: Diagnose the canal and side, rule out central causes and cervical vascular risk, then treat with canalith repositioning. The guideline gives a strong recommendation to treat posterior canal BPPV with a repositioning procedure and a strong recommendation against post-procedure postural restrictions [r1]. Observation with follow-up is an option for some patients, and vestibular rehabilitation is an option [r1]. Do not use routine imaging, vestibular testing or vestibular suppressants for typical BPPV [r1]. In people with concussion, treat BPPV as one of several causes of dizziness, and expect post-traumatic BPPV to need more manoeuvres, bilateral involvement and a higher chance of recurrence [r7,r4,r2]. Reassess within 1 month and educate on safety, recurrence and follow-up [r1].

medical.name: Observation with follow-up
medical.description: A guideline option for patients with BPPV, in whom the problem may settle spontaneously. The median untreated episode lasted 2 weeks, and only 8% of affected people in a survey had received effective treatment, so reassessment is needed [r1,r11].

medical.name: Vestibular suppressant drugs (antihistamines, benzodiazepines)
medical.description: The guideline recommends against routinely treating BPPV with vestibular suppressants, because the problem is mechanical and repositioning treats the cause [r1].

medical.name: Routine imaging or vestibular testing for typical BPPV
medical.description: The guideline recommends against imaging or vestibular testing when criteria for BPPV are met and there are no atypical features [r1].

medical.name: ENT or neurology referral for atypical, central or refractory cases
medical.description: Refer when the nystagmus or history is atypical, central signs are present, there is hearing loss, or symptoms persist despite repeated manoeuvres [r1,r8].

physio.name: Canalith repositioning (Epley manoeuvre) for posterior canal BPPV
physio.description: Move the patient through a sequence of head and body positions that uses gravity to return the crystals to the utricle. In a Cochrane review of 11 trials (745 patients), complete resolution was more common than with sham or control (OR 4.42, 95% CI 2.62–7.44; resolution rose from 21% to 56%), a positive Dix-Hallpike converted to negative more often (OR 9.62, 95% CI 6.0–15.42), and there were no serious adverse effects. Nausea during the manoeuvre occurred in 16.7%–32%, and recurrence was 36% [r6]. The guideline gives a strong recommendation to treat posterior canal BPPV with a repositioning procedure [r1].

physio.name: Alternative repositioning manoeuvres (Semont, Gans, Li)
physio.description: Epley was comparable to Semont, Gans and Li manoeuvres in a review of nine RCTs of low to very low certainty; Epley was better than Gans at 24 hours but not after 1 week [r13]. In the Cochrane review, Epley was superior to Brandt-Daroff exercises in one trial [r6].

physio.name: Horizontal canal manoeuvres after a supine roll test
physio.description: For horizontal canal BPPV, confirm the type with the supine roll test and use a canal-specific manoeuvre (for example the barbecue roll or Gufoni). The guideline recommends the roll test; evidence for specific horizontal-canal manoeuvres was not reviewed for this page [r1].

physio.name: Avoiding post-procedure postural restrictions
physio.description: The guideline makes a strong recommendation against post-procedure postural restrictions after canalith repositioning for posterior canal BPPV: the patient does not need to sleep upright or avoid head movement [r1].

physio.name: Vestibular rehabilitation
physio.description: A guideline option, self-administered or with a clinician, particularly for residual dizziness and balance after repositioning or when manoeuvres cannot be done [r1].

physio.name: Patient education, safety and follow-up
physio.description: Educate on the impact of BPPV on safety, the potential for recurrence and the importance of follow-up. Assess fall risk and reassess within 1 month [r1].

physio.name: Continuing to rely on rest or avoidance of provoking movements
physio.description: Avoiding positions does not treat the cause, which is mechanical. The guideline recommends repositioning as treatment and advises against post-procedure restrictions [r1].

education: BPPV is caused by tiny crystals in the wrong part of the inner ear. It is not dangerous in itself and it is treatable.
A simple manoeuvre moves the crystals back. Many people improve after one or two treatments, but it can come back, so you should know what to do if it does.
You do not need to keep your head still or sleep upright after the treatment.
Move carefully until you are better. Take care on stairs, ladders and when driving, and be aware that you may feel unsteady.
If you have a head injury, BPPV is only one possible cause of dizziness. Other causes can be treated too.
Seek urgent help for severe headache, double vision, slurred speech, weakness, constant vertigo, neck pain with dizziness, or hearing loss.

rehab.overview: Treatment is criteria-based and short. Stage 1 diagnoses the canal and treats it with repositioning. Stage 2 reassesses and repeats the manoeuvre if the Dix-Hallpike remains positive. Stage 3 treats residual dizziness and balance. Stage 4 returns the person to normal activity, and, after head injury, to the concussion return pathway. Dosages are typical clinical practice; the manoeuvre itself is supported by the Cochrane review and the guideline [r6,r1]. Do not impose post-treatment postural restrictions [r1].

stages.name: Diagnose and reposition
goals: Rule out central and vascular causes
Identify the canal and side with Dix-Hallpike or the supine roll test
precautions: Screen for central signs and cervical vascular risk before positioning [r8,r9]
Check neck range and tolerance; modify if the neck cannot tolerate extension [r6]
Warn about nausea during the manoeuvre (16.7%–32%) [r6]
Stop if neurological symptoms, severe headache or neck pain appear

exercises.name: Dix-Hallpike test on each side
exercises.dosage: Hold each side for at least 30 seconds, observing the eyes
exercises.cues: Head turned 45°, neck extended about 20°, affected ear down [r1]

exercises.name: Epley manoeuvre for the affected side
exercises.dosage: Hold each position until the vertigo and nystagmus settle plus about 30 seconds (clinical convention); repeat once or twice in the visit if still positive
exercises.cues: Move through the sequence smoothly, staying in each position until vertigo stops

exercises.name: Seated rest and re-sit
exercises.dosage: Sit upright slowly after the manoeuvre and rest for a few minutes
exercises.cues: No postural restrictions are needed afterwards [r1]

progressionCriteria: Typical BPPV confirmed and central causes excluded
Patient understands the plan and safety advice

stages.name: Reassess and repeat
goals: Document whether the Dix-Hallpike is still positive
Check other canals and the other ear
precautions: Post-traumatic BPPV often needs more manoeuvres and may be bilateral [r7,r2]

exercises.name: Repeat Dix-Hallpike on both sides
exercises.cues: Check for residual nystagmus and new horizontal canal findings

exercises.name: Repeat Epley or alternative manoeuvre
exercises.dosage: One to two manoeuvres per visit until the test is negative
exercises.cues: Consider the Semont or other manoeuvre if the Epley is unsuccessful [r13]

exercises.name: Supine roll test if Dix-Hallpike is negative but positional vertigo persists
exercises.cues: Look for horizontal nystagmus; treat horizontal canal BPPV with a specific manoeuvre [r1]

progressionCriteria: No provoked vertigo in bed rolling or looking up

stages.name: Residual dizziness and balance
goals: Resolve the residual unsteadiness after repositioning
precautions: Keep symptoms mild and settling within minutes
Take fall precautions for older or frail patients [r1]
Stop if headache or neurological symptoms appear

exercises.name: Single-leg stance
exercises.dosage: 3 × 30 seconds each side, eyes open then closed

exercises.name: Walking with head turns
exercises.dosage: 5 minutes, once or twice a day
exercises.cues: Smooth pace; turn the head gently

exercises.name: Gaze stabilisation (vestibulo-ocular reflex) exercise
exercises.dosage: Fix gaze on a target while turning the head, 3 × 30 seconds, daily
exercises.cues: Mild dizziness settling in a minute is acceptable

exercises.name: Habituation: slow repeated provoking movements
exercises.dosage: 5–10 repetitions, 2 times a day, only if still mildly provoking after repositioning
exercises.cues: Part of vestibular rehabilitation, an option in the guideline [r1]

progressionCriteria: No provoked vertigo on daily movements
Balance tests normal or near normal
Confident to return to usual activity

stages.name: Return to activity and follow-up
goals: Return to normal activity, work and driving
Link to the concussion return-to-sport pathway if relevant
precautions: If BPPV follows a concussion, return to sport follows the concussion pathway
Avoid sudden head movements in contact or at height until clear

exercises.name: Graded aerobic exercise below the symptom threshold
exercises.dosage: 20 minutes daily, increasing as tolerated (clinical convention for post-concussion exercise)

exercises.name: Neck mobility and posture work
exercises.dosage: 5–10 minutes, daily, if neck stiffness persists

exercises.name: Recurrence plan and education
exercises.cues: Recurrence occurred in about 36% after treatment, so teach early recognition [r6]

progressionCriteria: No provoked vertigo for at least 2 weeks
Return to normal activity, work and sport

criteria: No provoked vertigo with lying down, rolling in bed, looking up or bending, and a negative Dix-Hallpike on both sides [r1]
Normal balance and gait, including with head turns, with no residual dizziness on exercise
Concussion criteria met if BPPV followed a head injury: symptom-free at rest and on exertion with a completed staged return (clinical convention)
Neck able to tolerate extension and rotation without dizziness or pain
No central signs on neurological examination
tests: Dix-Hallpike and supine roll test on both sides [r1]
Single-leg stance and gait with head turns
Graded exercise test if concussion is also present [r16]
Review at 1 month to document resolution [r1]

prognosis: BPPV usually responds to repositioning. In the Cochrane review, complete resolution of vertigo rose from 21% to 56% after an Epley manoeuvre, and a positive Dix-Hallpike converted to negative in far more treated patients [r6]. Recurrence is common (36% in the Cochrane review and 38% in a tertiary series, with overall resolution of 76%) [r6,r2]. Post-traumatic BPPV may need more manoeuvres (RR 3.27 in one meta-analysis, mean 2.0 versus 1.3 in another series) and may recur more often (RR 2.91), although a large single-centre series found similar outcomes after trauma [r7,r4,r2]. Untreated, the median episode lasted 2 weeks in the population survey [r11]. A review describes a prolonged, refractory course after traumatic brain injury and a need for multidisciplinary care when BPPV coexists with other vestibular problems [r3].
prevention: Prevent head injury in the first place by following concussion prevention measures (see the concussion page); post-traumatic BPPV followed head trauma in about 8% of BPPV cases [r2].
Test for BPPV in every patient with dizziness after head injury, because it is treatable and can be missed [r12,r3].
Treat promptly with canalith repositioning rather than waiting. Only 8% of affected people received effective treatment in a survey [r11].
Teach patients to recognise recurrence and return early, and reassess within 1 month [r1].
Assess falls risk and home safety in older or frail patients [r1].
clinicalPearls: Test for BPPV in every person with dizziness after head injury. In 179 patients after mild traumatic brain injury, 10.6% had positional vertigo and BPPV was confirmed in 9, but it is easily missed among other concussion symptoms [r12].
Screen first. Rule out central causes (HINTS in continuous vertigo) and cervical vascular pathology before putting the neck into extension and rotation [r8,r9,r10].

Do not sell the Dix-Hallpike as a precise test. Its estimated sensitivity of 79% and specificity of 75% come from one study of very weak methodology; it is the accepted reference standard, so combine it with the history and the typical nystagmus [r14,r1].
Epley works, with resolution of 56% versus 21% and no post-treatment restrictions needed. Tell patients that recurrence of about 36% is common [r6,r1].
Expect post-traumatic BPPV to be harder: more manoeuvres, more bilateral cases and possibly more recurrence, though the data conflict [r7,r2,r4].
Do not give vestibular suppressants routinely, and do not order imaging for typical BPPV [r1].

animation.title: How post-traumatic BPPV happens and is treated

captions.text: Since a head knock, a patient has brief spinning vertigo when lying down.
In the Dix-Hallpike test, the clinician lies the patient back with the head turned and tipped.
The head position moves loose crystals in an inner ear canal, and vertigo and nystagmus begin.
The vertigo lasts less than a minute. It stops as the crystals settle.
Zooming into the right inner ear.
The inner ear has three canals. The posterior canal is the one most often affected.
Tiny crystals (otoconia) normally sit on the utricle.
After head trauma, some crystals come loose and drift into the posterior canal.
When the head tips back, they fall through the canal and drag the fluid, which deflects the cupula.
The brain gets a false signal of rotation, so the room seems to spin.
The Epley manoeuvre uses gravity to move the crystals back into the utricle.
Healthy: otoconia sit on the macula and the canal fluid is still.
Trauma loosens some otoconia from the macula.
They migrate into the posterior canal and settle in the long arm.
A head movement sends them sliding through the canal.
They drag the fluid and deflect the cupula, causing vertigo and nystagmus.
Repositioning returns the crystals to the utricle, and the vertigo stops.
